**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first time I tried to write a thousand words in one sitting, I stared at the blank page like it was a vast, untamed wilderness. A thousand words—how heavy they seemed, each one a brick in an invisible wall I had to build before the sun set. But then I realized: a thousand words is nothing. It’s the length of a long email, a short story, a rant about the state of the world at 2 a.m. It’s the number of steps between here and the coffee shop down the street if you walk slowly. It’s the number of excuses I’ve made to avoid starting.

So I start with this: *The cursor blinks like a metronome keeping time for a song no one is singing.*

And then the words come, not in a flood but in drips, like a leaky faucet in an old apartment. They collect in puddles of thought—some clear, some murky. I think about the way my grandmother’s hands looked when she peeled oranges, how the rind would curl into spirals that smelled like sunlight. I think about the first time I heard a song and felt like it was written just for the version of me that existed in that exact moment. I think about the way cities hum at night, a low electric lullaby that never quite lets you sleep.

There’s a myth that ideas are rare, that inspiration is a lightning bolt that strikes only the chosen few. But the truth is, inspiration is just noticing. It’s the way the barista always writes your name wrong on the cup, or the way your dog watches you eat like he’s memorizing the taste of food he’ll never have. It’s the crack in the sidewalk where a weed grows, stubborn and green. A thousand words can hold all of that.

I used to think writing was about having something to say. Now I think it’s about saying something anyway—even if it’s just *I don’t know, but here’s the shape of my not-knowing.*

Some days, the words feel like a river, rushing so fast I can barely keep up. Other days, they’re like pulling teeth—each one a struggle, each sentence a small rebellion against the silence. But the river and the desert both have leur beauty. The river carves canyons. The desert teaches you to listen.

I remember reading that J.R.R. Tolkien once said *Fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason.* And I think about how we’re all, in some way, storytelling creatures. We narrate our lives to ourselves, turn our regrets into tragedies, our small joys into comedies. A thousand words is just a slice of that—one scene in the play, one verse in the song.

What if I told you that right now, somewhere, a stranger is thinking about the same color of blue you are? Or that the person who invented the paperclip probably didn’t think it would hold together the scattered pages of a love letter one day? We’re all connected by these small, silent threads.

I wonder if the first person to ever write a word down knew how heavy words would become. How they could start wars or end them. How they could make a child laugh or an old man cry. How they could be both nothing (just ink, just pixels) and everything (a universe built from 26 letters).

This is the 500th word. Halfway. I could stop here, but I won’t. Because the magic isn’t in the destination—it’s in the walking. It’s in the way the path twists when you least expect it, in the detours that turn out to be the point all along.

I think about time. How a minute can stretch into eternity when you’re waiting for news, or collapse into nothing when you’re lost in a book. How a lifetime can feel like a single breath when you’re old. We measure our lives in words, in heartbeats, in the slow decay of things we thought would last forever.

There’s a Japanese word, *komorebi*, which means the sunlight filtering through the leaves of a tree. There’s no exact English equivalent, which is proof that some things need a whole new word to be understood. Maybe that’s why we write—to find the words for the things that don’t have them yet.

I used to be afraid of blank pages. Now I see them as invitations. *Fill me," they whisper. "You have a thousand words inside you. Let them out."*

And so I do.

The last time I counted, this was word 742. I have 258 left, give or take. I could fill them with grand philosophies or tiny observations. I could list all the things I’ve lost or all the things I hope to find. I could describe the taste of the first sip of coffee in the morning, bitter and perfect. I could tell you about the time I saw a shooting star and made a wish I’ve already forgotten.

But maybe the point isn’t what the words say. Maybe it’s that they exist at all. That in a world where so much is temporary, words are one of the few things that can outlast us. That a thousand years from now, someone might read these words and think, *Oh, there was a person. They were here.*

So here I am. Here we are. Alive, for now. Typing, scribbling, speaking, shouting into the void and hoping the void shouts back.

Word 900. The finish line is in sight, but I don’t want to rush. There’s comfort in the rhythm of it—the tap of keys, the hum of the laptop, the way my mind jumps from thought to thought like a stone skipping across water.

I think about how we’re all just stories in the end. And stories are made of words. So here’s a thousand of mine, strung together like beads on a thread. Some are shiny. Some are dull. All of them are true, in their own way.

And now, the last few. The period at the end of the sentence. The deep breath after the long run.

A thousand words. Done.

(Exactly 1,000. Give or take a few.)
